specPoints.text: explain how molecules in a gas have random motion and that they exert a force, and hence a pressure, on the walls of a container

primer.text: Pressure is not a substance pushing — it is quadrillions of tiny collisions adding up. This note follows one gas molecule from collision to collision and shows how random motion plus wall impacts produce a steady, measurable pressure on every wall of the container.

lessons.title: Random motion of gas molecules
lessons.opening: Gas molecules never rest: they travel in straight lines at hundreds of metres per second until a collision sends them off in a new direction. The motion is random — no direction is preferred — and that randomness is the seed of every gas law.
keyPoints: Gas molecules move with rapid, random motion in all directions.
Between collisions each molecule travels in a straight line at constant speed.
Collisions with other molecules and with the container walls change a molecule's direction.
No direction of travel is preferred because the motion is random.
The random directions average out, so the gas fills its container uniformly.

low.restatement: Picture trillions of ping-pong balls in a box, all flying fast, bouncing off each other and the walls forever. Each ball's path is straight between bounces, and no direction is special.
low.analogy: A popcorn kernel panic inside a sealed pan: every corn rockets off in whatever direction its last bounce dictated.
low.examPointer: The word 'random' must be paired with 'rapid' — questions usually want the motion described as fast and in all directions.

medium.restatement: Kinetic theory models molecules as point masses undergoing elastic collisions, so speeds stay high and directions randomise at every impact. The velocity distribution is isotropic: summed over all molecules, the mean velocity vector is zero even though the mean speed is large, which is why the gas as a whole stays put while its molecules race.
medium.analogy: A swarm of bees in a marquee: individually each bee dashes purposefully, but the swarm's centre never moves because every direction cancels its opposite.
medium.examPointer: If asked why the gas's net momentum is zero, answer with the cancellation of random directions — individual speeds are far from zero.

check.stem: How do gas molecules move between collisions?

options.text: in straight lines at constant speed
options.explanation: With no forces acting between collisions, straight-line motion holds.

options.text: in curved paths pulled by gravity
options.explanation: Gravity's bend is negligible at molecular scale and time-frame.

options.text: in orbits around other molecules
options.explanation: Molecules do not orbit; they collide.

options.text: they hover and vibrate in place
options.explanation: Hovering describes nothing; vibrating in place is the solid picture.

check.stem: What does 'random motion' mean for a gas?

options.text: the molecules' directions of travel have no preferred direction
options.explanation: Randomness is about direction distribution, not chaos of speed.

options.text: the molecules all travel at random different speeds in one direction
options.explanation: One shared direction is exactly what randomness excludes.

options.text: the molecules stop and start at random times
options.explanation: Molecules keep moving between collisions; they do not pause.

options.text: the molecules swap identities during collisions
options.explanation: Model molecules are conserved, not exchanged.

check.stem: Why does a gas fill its container uniformly?

options.text: random motion in all directions carries molecules into every region equally
options.explanation: Directional randomness plus free travel spreads the gas evenly.

options.text: gravity spreads the molecules evenly
options.explanation: Gravity would pool them at the bottom if it dominated.

options.text: the molecules expand in size
options.explanation: Molecule size never changes.

options.text: the walls pull the molecules towards them
options.explanation: Walls receive collisions; they do not attract.

check.stem: A molecule hits another molecule head-on and bounces back. What has changed for it?

options.text: its direction of travel has changed
options.explanation: Collisions redirect; in the elastic model speeds are conserved overall.

options.text: it has stopped moving
options.explanation: A collision transfers motion, it does not end it.

options.text: it has become a liquid molecule
options.explanation: State is a bulk property, not a single-molecule transformation.

options.text: its speed permanently halves at every collision
options.explanation: Elastic collisions conserve total kinetic energy.

check.stem: Why can we say the gas as a whole has zero net velocity even though its molecules race about?

options.text: the random directions cancel: for every molecule going one way, another goes the opposite way
options.explanation: Vector sums over random directions average to zero.

options.text: all molecules are actually at rest between collisions
options.explanation: They move fast between collisions.

options.text: the container absorbs their motion
options.explanation: Walls only reflect momentum; they do not swallow the net (which is already zero).

options.text: speed and velocity are the same thing
options.explanation: Velocity is a vector; the average vector cancels while speed remains.

check.stem: State what is meant by random motion of gas molecules.
check.modelAnswer: The molecules move rapidly with no preferred direction of travel, flying in straight lines between collisions that redirect them.

check.stem: State two things that change a molecule's direction of travel.
check.modelAnswer: Collisions with other molecules and collisions with the container walls both redirect a molecule.

check.stem: Explain why the random motion of molecules does not make the gas drift towards one side of the container.
check.modelAnswer: Because the motion is random, every direction of travel is equally represented among the molecules. For any molecule heading towards the left wall at any instant, another is heading right, another up and another down, so the momentum flows cancel. The gas's centre of mass therefore stays put even though each molecule is moving fast.

check.stem: A perfume bottle is opened at the front of a classroom. Using the kinetic model, explain why the smell reaches the back but takes noticeably longer than a sound wave.
check.modelAnswer: Perfume molecules leave the bottle moving fast but in random directions, so they travel by many short straight flights redirected at every collision — a random walk. Sound is an ordered wave carried by the air's existing molecules, so it crosses the room far faster than the diffusive random walk of the perfume molecules.

lessons.title: From wall collisions to pressure
lessons.opening: Every time a molecule strikes a wall it delivers a tiny impulse. Multiply by trillions of molecules and billions of strikes per second and the bombardment becomes a smooth, steady push — the gas's pressure.
keyPoints: Each molecule striking a container wall exerts a tiny force on it.
Pressure is the total force from all collisions divided by the wall's area.
Countless collisions per second make the wall force steady and measurable.
Higher molecular speeds or more frequent collisions give a greater pressure.
Pressure acts at right angles to every wall, on all sides of the container.

low.restatement: One molecule's hit is negligible, but trillions of hits every second add up to a smooth push on each wall. That push spread over the wall's area is the pressure the gauge reads.
low.analogy: Rain on a roof: one drop is nothing, but a steady downpour produces a constant drumming force across the whole surface.
low.examPointer: Tie the mechanism in one chain — collision, force, total force over area, pressure — because exam marks are awarded for the chain, not the endpoint.

medium.restatement: On impact a molecule's momentum reverses, so by Newton's second law the wall experiences an impulse; summing impulses per unit time gives an average force, and force per unit area is pressure. The isotropy of random motion makes this pressure equal on all walls, and it scales with both the collision rate and the momentum change per collision.
medium.analogy: A firing squad of ping-pong balls aimed from every angle: no single ball dents the armour, but the sustained hail presses on it from every side equally.
medium.examPointer: Quote Newton's second law in impulse form when explaining the force — 'the wall reverses the molecule's momentum' — because that is the rigorous version of 'the molecule pushes the wall'.

check.stem: Where does the pressure of a gas come from?

options.text: molecules colliding with the container walls
options.explanation: Wall bombardment delivers the steady force we call pressure.

options.text: the weight of the molecules only
options.explanation: Weight plays no role in a sealed container's gas pressure at this scale.

options.text: molecules rubbing against each other
options.explanation: Friction between molecules is not the pressure mechanism.

options.text: the walls attracting the molecules
options.explanation: Attraction is negligible; impacts do the work.

check.stem: What happens to the momentum of a molecule when it bounces off a wall?

options.text: it reverses, so the wall receives an impulse
options.explanation: Momentum reversal at the wall is the pressure mechanism.

options.text: it doubles and stays the same direction
options.explanation: The bounce reverses the perpendicular component.

options.text: it disappears into the wall
options.explanation: Momentum is transferred to the wall, not destroyed.

options.text: nothing — walls are passive
options.explanation: The wall feels every impact.

check.stem: Why is the pressure the same on all walls of a sealed box of gas?

options.text: random motion is equally likely towards every wall
options.explanation: Directional randomness makes the bombardment isotropic.

options.text: the walls are made of the same material
options.explanation: Wall material is irrelevant to gas pressure.

options.text: gravity presses the gas equally sideways
options.explanation: Gravity acts downwards; it does not equalise side walls.

options.text: the molecules all orbit the box's centre
options.explanation: There are no orbits in the kinetic model.

check.stem: A gas is squeezed into half its volume at constant temperature. What happens to the wall-collision rate?

options.text: collisions per second on each wall increase, raising the pressure
options.explanation: Less space means shorter flight times and more frequent impacts.

options.text: collisions become rarer, raising the pressure
options.explanation: Rarer collisions would lower the pressure.

options.text: the collision rate is unchanged
options.explanation: Compression shortens paths, so the rate must rise.

options.text: collisions stop once compressed
options.explanation: Molecules never stop moving at ordinary temperatures.

check.stem: A sealed can is heated. Using the kinetic model, explain why the pressure inside rises.

options.text: faster molecules hit the walls harder and more often
options.explanation: Both the impulse per hit and the hit rate rise with temperature.

options.text: the molecules grow larger when heated
options.explanation: Sizes are fixed; speeds are what change.

options.text: heating removes molecules from the walls
options.explanation: The molecule count is unchanged in a sealed can.

options.text: the can's area shrinks when hot
options.explanation: Thermal expansion of the can is negligible and opposite in effect.

check.stem: State what exerts the force on the walls of a gas container.
check.modelAnswer: The molecules of the gas exert the force, through their collisions with the walls.

check.stem: State how pressure is calculated from the wall force.
check.modelAnswer: Pressure equals the total force on a wall divided by the area of that wall.

check.stem: Explain why a collision with a wall delivers an impulse to the wall even though the molecule is microscopic.
check.modelAnswer: The molecule arrives with momentum towards the wall and leaves with momentum away from it, so its momentum changes. By Newton's second law a change of momentum requires a force, and by Newton's third law the molecule and wall push on each other equally. The wall therefore receives an impulse — tiny, but delivered by trillions of molecules every second.

check.stem: A party balloon left near a fire swells and may burst. Use the kinetic model to explain the swelling in terms of wall collisions.
check.modelAnswer: Heating makes the air molecules inside the balloon faster, so they strike the rubber walls harder and more often. The greater steady bombardment pushes the rubber outward, stretching the balloon until its tension balances the higher internal pressure — or it bursts if the rubber cannot stretch far enough.

glossary.definition: The model explaining gas behaviour by the rapid random motion of its molecules.
A collision in which total kinetic energy is conserved.
Force per unit area, produced in gases by molecular collisions with the walls.
